Starting point

Your declared mandate covers pre-seed, seed and Series A investments, with cheques from €50,000 to €100 million, a typical cheque of €3 million, and flexibility to lead, co-invest or follow. Your stated focus includes fintech, enterprise software, B2B SaaS and Africa; regulated businesses are a plus, while insurance, gambling and adult content are excluded.

The plan below is therefore staged around pipeline development, evidence-led diligence, disciplined deployment and follow-on capacity. It is a framework rather than a fixed allocation model because your annual capital budget, preferred number of positions, maximum exposure per company and fintech sub-themes are not yet established.

Month 1 — Set the investment boundaries

• Confirm the annual capital budget for Nigerian fintech.
• Set a target range for the number of new positions.
• Define a maximum initial allocation and maximum total exposure per company.
• Decide how much capital should remain available for follow-ons.
• Divide the fintech opportunity into sub-themes you want to pursue, such as payments, infrastructure, lending, compliance, embedded finance or financial software.
• Confirm which risks are acceptable and which are hard exclusions beyond insurance, gambling and adult content.

Output: a one-page Nigerian fintech mandate with deployment limits, target sub-themes and exclusion criteria.

Month 2 — Build the sourcing system

• Create a pipeline of Nigerian companies across pre-seed, seed and Series A.
• Separate opportunities into three groups: companies ready for first review, companies requiring more evidence and companies outside the mandate.
• Record stage, geography, business model, regulatory exposure, customer type, founding-team capability and capital needs for each company.
• Establish a consistent first-screen process so that every company is assessed against the same criteria.

Output: a live pipeline with clear next actions and reasons for inclusion or exclusion.

Month 3 — Run first-stage screening

For each company that passes the initial screen, establish:

• The specific customer problem and who pays.
• Product maturity and whether the product is in production.
• Regulatory status, licences, partnerships or dependencies.
• Early customer evidence, including retention, repeat usage and concentration.
• Revenue model, gross-margin logic and key operating costs.
• Founder capabilities, relevant domain expertise and enterprise-sales ability.
• Current stage, round structure and intended use of capital.

Use a simple decision path: advance, request evidence, monitor or pass. Do not treat a compelling market narrative as a substitute for operating evidence.

Output: a first-stage diligence record for each active opportunity.

Month 4 — Concentrate on the strongest evidence

• Select a smaller group for deeper work rather than progressing every company equally.
• Test whether reported traction is supported by dated operating data, customer references or financial records.
• Distinguish regulated-market advantage from regulatory dependency.
• Examine whether growth is driven by durable customer demand or by incentives, subsidies or one-off contracts.
• Identify the principal failure modes for each business: credit losses, fraud, compliance, liquidity, distribution costs, concentration or technical execution.

Output: a focused diligence pipeline with explicit evidence gaps and decision owners.

Month 5 — Conduct investment committee diligence

For each company under serious consideration, prepare an investment memo covering:

• Problem and product.
• Market and competitive position.
• Customer acquisition and retention.
• Unit economics and path to contribution margin.
• Regulatory and compliance position.
• Technology, security and operational resilience.
• Founder-market fit and hiring requirements.
• Financing history, current round and use of funds.
• Downside cases and conditions that would invalidate the thesis.

Require the company to identify which claims are evidenced, which remain self-reported and which are not yet known.

Output: decision-ready memos with a clear list of unresolved questions.

Month 6 — Make the first deployment decisions

• Deploy only where the core thesis and critical risks are sufficiently evidenced.
• Use smaller initial positions when the opportunity fits the mandate but material execution or regulatory uncertainty remains.
• Reserve a defined amount for follow-ons before committing the full annual budget.
• Where you are not leading, confirm that the lead investor’s diligence is aligned with your own key risks.
• Record the reason for investing, the evidence supporting it and the conditions for continued support.

Output: the first portfolio positions, or a documented decision to wait where the evidence is not sufficient.

Month 7 — Expand selectively

• Replenish the pipeline with companies that fit the refined sub-themes.
• Prioritise businesses with clear customer pull, credible regulatory positioning and strong technical or domain capability.
• Compare new opportunities with existing holdings before deploying, rather than assessing each company in isolation.
• Avoid concentration in one revenue model, customer segment, licence dependency or distribution channel.

Output: a second deployment shortlist that improves portfolio diversification rather than simply increasing deal count.

Month 8 — Establish portfolio reporting

For each holding, track a small set of comparable indicators:

• Revenue and revenue growth.
• Active customers and retention.
• Gross margin or contribution margin where relevant.
• Cash position and monthly burn.
• Runway.
• Regul
